front: What is ACID in one sentence?
back: Transaction guarantees: all-or-nothing writes, valid states, predictable concurrency, survive crashes — Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann, Ch. 7).

front: What is Dirty read?
back: read uncommitted data from another tx; rolled-back rows looked real.

front: What is Non-repeatable read?
back: same SELECT twice in one tx returns different rows (other tx committed an update).

front: What is Phantom read?
back: same range query twice returns different row *count* (inserts/deletes committed by others).

front: What is Lost update?
back: two txs read same value, both write; one overwrite silently lost (not always classified as "anomaly" but most common app bug).

front: What is Write skew?
back: two txs read disjoint rows, write constraints that together violate an invariant (classic: on-call calendar — two people both think they're sole on-call).

front: In ACID, what is Atomicity?
back: Crash mid-transaction — half applied? — Undo log + rollback; WAL replay

front: In ACID, what is Consistency?
back: Invalid states possible? — Constraints, FKs, triggers, app invariants

front: In ACID, what is Isolation?
back: Concurrent txs see each other's partial work? — Locks, MVCC, isolation levels

front: In ACID, what is Durability?
back: Committed survives power loss? — WAL (Write-Ahead Log) + fsync

front: For PostgreSQL in ACID, what is the key fact?
back: READ COMMITTED — Each statement gets fresh snapshot

front: For MySQL InnoDB in ACID, what is the key fact?
back: REPEATABLE READ — Consistent reads via undo; gap locks on indexes

front: For SQL Server in ACID, what is the key fact?
back: READ COMMITTED — Row versioning optional (RCSI)

front: For SQLite in ACID, what is the key fact?
back: SERIALIZABLE — Single-writer; still see SQLITE_BUSY

front: What are the production-safe defaults for ACID?
back: App must retry on 40001 serialization failure — framework rarely does this for you.

front: At isolation level READ UNCOMMITTED, which anomalies are possible?
back: Dirty read: ✓ possible | Non-repeatable read: ✓ | Phantom read: ✓

front: At isolation level READ COMMITTED, which anomalies are possible?
back: Dirty read: ✗ | Non-repeatable read: ✓ possible | Phantom read: ✓

front: At isolation level REPEATABLE READ, which anomalies are possible?
back: Dirty read: ✗ | Non-repeatable read: ✗ | Phantom read: ✓ possible*

front: At isolation level SERIALIZABLE, which anomalies are possible?

front: Symptom: Random 40001 / deadlock — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: pg_stat_database deadlocks; MySQL SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS · Fix: Shorten txs; consistent lock order; retry with backoff

front: Symptom: "It worked once, then duplicate" — what do you check and fix?

front: Symptom: Long-running open tx bloat — what do you check and fix?

front: Symptom: Phantom counts in reports — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: RR not enough on PG without SERIALIZABLE · Fix: Raise isolation or SELECT … FOR UPDATE on range

front: Symptom: Balance wrong after concurrent updates — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Lost update — no locking · Fix: FOR UPDATE or atomic UPDATE … SET x = x + 1

front: Symptom: Migration "half applied" — what do you check and fix?

front: Gotcha with ACID: what silently fails?
back: Autocommit + read-modify-write — three separate statements = three transactions on READ COMMITTED. Classic inventory oversell.

front: When should you NOT use ACID?
back: Cross-DB atomicity — no single ACID tx spans Postgres + Redis + S3. Use outbox/saga. SERIALIZABLE everywhere — throughput cost + retry storms; use for narrow critical paths. Assuming ORM @Transactional fixes isolation — it opens a tx; level is still DB default unless you SET it.

front: What is ARIES in one sentence?
back: One-line: industry-standard WAL recovery algorithm ( steal + no-force ) — analysis → redo → undo after crash; underpins SQL Server, Db2, and many enterprise engines.

front: Explain the mental model of ARIES (how the system thinks).
back: ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics) defines how to recover after crash when the buffer pool uses steal (uncommitted pages may flush) and no-force (committed pages need not be on disk before commit ack). Safety comes from WAL (Write-Ahead Log): log record before page change.

front: When should you NOT use ARIES?
back: Not an app-level pattern — you don't implement ARIES; you tune the engine that already does. Embedded SQLite — simpler recovery; still WAL-based but not full ARIES paper.

front: What is BASE in one sentence?
back: One-line: distributed-systems tradeoff label — Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency — opposite emphasis from ACID; know what you're giving up.

front: Explain the mental model of BASE (how the system thinks).
back: ACID optimizes single-node transactional correctness. BASE describes many distributed / NoSQL designs that prefer availability under partition (CAP theorem intuition): respond even when stale; accept that replicas converge eventually.

front: What is GridFS in one sentence?
back: One-line: MongoDB's convention for storing files >16MB BSON limit — chunks in fs.files + fs.chunks; stream in/out; not a general filesystem.

front: Explain the mental model of GridFS (how the system thinks).
back: BSON documents cap at 16MB. GridFS splits a file into 255KB chunks (default), storing metadata in fs.files and binary chunks in fs.chunks (default bucket prefix fs).

back: Upload stream ──► fs.files (metadata: filename, length, uploadDate)

front: Symptom: Slow listing — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Missing index on filename · Fix: Index fs.files.filename; query by _id when possible

front: Symptom: Orphan chunks after failed upload — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Partial upload · Fix: Abort stream; delete incomplete file doc; periodic cleanup job

front: Symptom: 16MB error still — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Not using GridFS · Fix: Any single document field still limited — only file payload is chunked

front: Symptom: Replica lag on large upload — what do you check and fix?
back: Check: Many chunk inserts · Fix: Increase chunk size; upload off-peak; use S3 for huge media

front: Symptom: MD5 mismatch (legacy) — what do you check and fix?

front: Symptom: Memory spike on download — what do you check and fix?

front: Gotcha with GridFS: what silently fails?
back: GridFS ≠ S3 — expensive at TB scale; object storage + CDN is cheaper for static media.

front: When should you NOT use GridFS?
back: Small blobs (< few MB) — embed BinData in document or store URL to S3. Full-text search on binary — extract text sidecar collection. Need POSIX semantics — use object storage or NFS.

front: What is OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) in one sentence?
back: Read-heavy analytics — scans, aggregates, GROUP BY across dimensions — optimized for dashboards and BI, not row-by-row checkout. Contrast OLTP: many small writes, index-point lookups, ACID transactions.

front: What is WAL (Write-Ahead Log) in one sentence?
back: Append-only durability journal: log the intent before mutating data pages — Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann, Ch. 3).

front: What is Log sequence number (LSN)?
back: monotonic pointer; pages record *last WAL applied* so recovery knows what's stale.

front: What is Checkpoint?
back: periodic marker: "all changes before LSN X are on disk." Truncates replay window.

front: Explain the mental model of WAL (Write-Ahead Log) (how the system thinks).
back: Every durable DB must survive crash mid-write. WAL is the contract: log record hits stable storage first, then in-memory/dirty pages may change. On restart, replay log from last checkpoint forward; undo incomplete transactions.

front: Symptom: Spiky write latency every N min — what do you check and fix?

front: Symptom: "could not write to WAL" / PANIC — what do you check and fix?

front: Gotcha with WAL (Write-Ahead Log): what silently fails?

front: What is WiredTiger storage engine in one sentence?
back: MongoDB's default storage engine since 4.2 — B-tree docs, MVCC, checkpointed durability, cache-bound performance — MongoDB manual + Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann, log-structured ideas).

front: What is Checkpoints?
back: consistent on-disk snapshot every storage.wiredTiger.engineConfig.checkpoint=(wait, seconds); crash recovery = last checkpoint + journal replay (WAL (Write-Ahead Log) family).

front: What is Journal?
back: 100ms commit interval default (journal.commitIntervalMs); group commit like Postgres.

front: What is Cache?
back: single big WT cache (cacheSizeGB); not the filesystem page cache alone — working set must fit or I/O explodes.
